Tracing Narnia: How the Landscapes of Northern Ireland Shaped CS Lewis’s Fantasy Realm

As anticipation builds for upcoming screen adaptations of *The Chronicles of Narnia*, travellers and literature fans alike are looking back at the real-world geographies that helped shape Belfast-born author CS Lewis’s magical kingdom. From the bustling streets of east Belfast to the dramatic peaks of the Mourne Mountains, Northern Ireland’s distinct topography left an indelible mark on the writer's childhood and creative imagination.

Exploring the Lewis Trail in Belfast

In east Belfast, reminders of Lewis and his literary legacy are woven into the urban fabric. CS Lewis Square, located in the Holywood Arches neighbourhood, features a walking trail populated by metal sculptures of beloved characters including Mr and Mrs Beaver and Mr Tumnus, anchored by a prominent statue of Aslan. Nearby, St Mark’s Church on the Holywood Road houses a replica of a brass lion’s head doorknob from its historic rectory, which many associate with the inspiration for Aslan. Further down the leafy Circular Road stands Little Lea, the large redbrick home where Lewis lived from 1905. The expansive rooms and long corridors of this childhood home directly influenced descriptions of the magical portals found in *The Magician’s Nephew* and *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*.

From Countryside Walks to the Mourne Mountains

Growing up, Lewis and his brother Warnie had extensive freedom to explore the hills and woodland glens framing the city. The dramatic topography leading up from Belmont Road towards Whitespots Country Park offered sweeping vistas over the plain of Down. Most notably, Lewis once remarked to his brother that the view from the Mournes above Rostrevor, looking down over Carlingford Lough, represented his personal vision of Narnia. That sentiment is commemorated on a bench within Kilbroney Forest Park. Additionally, scholars continue to debate whether the dramatic ruins of Dunluce Castle or the clifftop Mussenden Temple at Downhill Demesne served as the true architectural inspiration for Cair Paravel, Narnia's royal castle.

Practical Implications and Reader Verification

For those planning to explore these literary landmarks, understanding what is officially documented versus what remains a matter of scholarly discussion is helpful:

  • Confirmed Locations: CS Lewis Square, St Mark's Church, and Little Lea (exterior viewable from iron gates) are accessible physical sites in east Belfast. Kilbroney Forest Park in Rostrevor features the official commemorative bench marking Lewis's stated connection to the Mourne Mountains.
  • Scholarship and Interpretation: Exact inspirations for specific fictional settings—such as the precise viewpoint for the Whitespots country park or whether Dunluce Castle versus Downhill Demesne inspired Cair Paravel—remain subjects of ongoing discussion among literary experts and fans rather than explicitly documented coordinates by the author.
  • Upcoming Media Releases: Netflix has announced that its upcoming adaptation, *Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew*, is scheduled for a cinematic release on 12 February 2027, followed by its streaming release on Netflix on 2 April.

Readers seeking to verify these details and plan travel itineraries can consult the original travel feature and cultural reporting published by The Guardian.
